newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's U.N. envoy Kharrazi named foreign minister.
newsitem.headline: Iran's U.N. envoy Kharrazi named foreign minister.

text.p: Kamal Kharrazi, nominated as foreign minister by Iran's President Mohammad Khatami on Tuesday, has been the country's ambassador to the United Nations since 1989.
If confirmed by parliament Kharrazi, 53, would replace veteran Ali Akbar Velayati, a soft-spoken paediatrician who has been the main international voice of the Islamic republic since December 1981.
As ambassador to the world body, Kharrazi was pivotal in putting together the agreement that led to the freeing in the early 1990s of Western hostages in Lebanon, diplomats say.
After university studies in his hometown Tehran, Kharrazi went to the United States in 1972 where he lived until 1979, the year of Iran's Islamic revolution.
There he earned a doctorate in education and gained revolutionary credentials as a leader of Islamist students opposed to the rule of the pro-Western Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Some diplomats said Kharrazi's appointment could give Tehran's foreign policy a stronger focus towards Washington.

But they added Kharrazi was a loyal technocrat unlikely to herald major changes in foreign policy, the realm of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Khamenei has rejected the possibility of a thaw in relations with the United States.

Kharrazi is on record as having said last November that no dialogue was possible then with the United States, Iran's arch-foe since militant students stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran in 1979 and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
After returning to Iran from the United States, Kharrazi held various positions until 1980, including director of the Centre for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults.
During the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq war he was in charge of propaganda and headed the country's official news agency IRNA from 1980 to 1989.

Reports that Kharrazi could be nominated have drawn criticism from some hardliners, with the Jomhuri Eslami newspaper blasting the choice as not "revolutionary enough" and calling for a "thorough spring cleaning" at the foreign ministry.

But Iranian analysts said Kharrazi had worked closely with Velayati, who is politically allied to the conservatives, and was expected to get the conservative-dominated parliament's vote of confidence.
